Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I thank my colleagues. I will finish just as quickly as possible.
The native community, I think, has to be brought into the process. I am anxious to listen to as many native community leaders as possible with respect to the correctional system and how it impacts on natives in our
November 4, 1991

system. I am also deeply concerned about women in the prison system, women offenders, and whether the programs are adequate. I do not think they are in many cases. I hope that this bill, through amendment, will have a positive impact in this category.
We are also going to have to do something about increasing the number of experts in the whole system itself. We just do not have enough trained people to work with severely disturbed inmates, severely handicapped inmates and the violent offenders.
I know that in psychiatry and in medicine and in psychology this part of their regiment and this part of their professional field is one that most shy away from. There is not much glamour and money in it and many of them treat it as an almost hopeless dead-end kind of professional practice. It does not have to be that way. We have to encourage more and better people to become involved in the correctional service and also with the National Parole Board itself.
Those are some of my concerns about this bill. I simply want to conclude by saying that there is much more I would like to have said but I do not want to indulge on the time of the House because I know my time is up. All one has to do is watch the American TV programs. Every state prosecutor and every judge who is up for re-election in New York state says: "I am tough on law and order. I put x number of people away behind bars. I kept x number of people behind bars for 20 years or 50 years or whatever it is".
Keep in mind that politicians can very easily stand up at election time or just before an election or in a pre-election period and preach the virtues of being tough with offenders in society and yet if you look at the reality and, as I said at the beginning of my speech, at the real causes of crime in our society, it is little wonder that we are really emphasizing the wrong thing.
We are not really getting to the causes of crime before it is committed. We are not trying to do something about poverty, about slums, about lack of education, violence on television, violence in the home, sexual molestation in the home. All of these things are what ultimately lead to the prosecutor, the defence attorney and the judge. We are left, we meaning the Correction Service of Canada and the Parole Board, with finding a way of
Government Orders
trying to deal with these people so that we can bring them back into society as law-abiding, useful citizens.
Longer sentences, the absence of parole, supervision and no release before expiry, are not going to reduce the crime rate. I do not have any divine knowledge on the subject, all I have to do is look at the facts and figures before us in the media day in and day out to know that in the United States and in other countries that is not the case. You can be tough on law and order in the courts and in the jails and yet the crime rate continues to increase.
In conclusion, one of the profound ironies of the 20th century is that Europe, which gave the world two great world wars in which millions of people lost their lives, innocent civilians lost their lives, is a far safer place to live at night on the streets no matter where than the western world which has been at relative peace in the political sense, in terms of war. Violence on the streets is increasing, violence in some areas of the United States is virtually out of control and now there are indications that in our larger cities in particular in Canada, violent crime is not out of control, but it is certainly on the increase and causing the citizens of our country grave concern.
Our number one concern is public safety, but we are also very concerned that this bill does not mislead the public, certainly at second reading, into thinking that by simply passing it we are somehow going to reduce the crime rate. It is going to take a lot more than that.
Mr. John Nunziata (York South

Weston): Mr. Speaker, the member seemed to misrepresent my position with regard to parole and the whole issue of whether parole should be abolished altogether. I should remind the member that the Law Reform Commission of Canada and a number of other groups in the criminal justice area have debated and discussed the idea of the abolition of parole. A number of prominent criminal lawyers have recommended the abolition of parole. Inmate groups have also supported the abolition of parole. The inmates do not like the uncertainty that is associated with lengthy sentences and the uncertainty of when they might be released on parole.
To accompany the abolition of parole, I am sure the member will agree, and he is not misrepresenting my position, you would have to reform sentencing at the same time. Let me just take a hypothetical situation. If

November 4, 1991
Government Orders
we are dealing with armed robbery, the average sentence may be nine years. The average length of time served in a penitentiary may be four or five years. Those who are advocating the abolition of parole say when you abolish parole you would also bring into line sentences so that you would take the average length of time served and make that the new sentence for armed robbery, for example. The maximum sentence for armed robbery would become five years as opposed to nine years.
I am not advocating lengthier sentences in a general way in the abolition of parole but rather the abolition of parole with a reform of the sentencing structure. In certain areas sentencing ought to be reformed and sentences ought to be increased. For example, if you drink and drive in Canada and if you are convicted for the second time, you automatically serve seven days or a week in jail. There is a mandatory period of incarceration, and yet if you are caught for the second, third, fourth, fifth time and convicted of selling drugs to kids in school yards, there is no minimum sentence. It does not make any sense at all why a drug pusher should not be treated at least as severely as someone who drinks and drives.
At sentencing.
At sentencing, that is correct.
We should reform that too?

The reform should be here now. Let me close by asking the member a question with regard to the position of his party. The New Democratic Party traditionally has favoured, or its philosophy is more supporting of, inmates rather than the protection of society. What I sense from the member's submission is that he is not seeking greater rights and more lenient sentences for inmates. He is not recommending that our prisons be emptied.
There seems to be a shift in the position of the New Democratic Party toward an emphasis or priority placed on public safety and that aspect of the criminal justice system. Perhaps the member could comment.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for his question. I want to make a point very clear, that where we have advocated lesser sentences or
greater acceleration through the prison system, is in the non-violent area. We believe, and I continue to believe, that we have far too many people in prison today who could be released and be no threat to anybody else in society. I am not saying they should be free, but we believe that they should go through the system faster, to halfway houses, do community service work, do public service work. If they are found guilty of very large frauds or serious frauds, so-called white collar crime, maybe at sentencing a prohibition of staying out of the business community for three, four, five years after release could be part of the sentence. We still maintain that there are people behind bars today who should not be there because they are non-violent and they would not be a risk to society.
We have never been opposed to being severe in our sentencing of those who are violent and those who continue to show violence while they are in the prison system. We do believe that no matter how mean or miserable a human being may be, and we are not perfect beings-and as one philosopher said, we are the only beings capable of reason and not rational beings-we still think that there is often hope that people will rehabilitate themselves and can re-enter society. Emphasis should be put on that, but not ahead of public safety and the security of law-abiding citizens, but that other process should be part of the correctional system.
That I think is very important and that is our position on it.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the member for clarification in his response to my colleague from York South-Weston. He seemed to be suggesting that white collar crime was not really putting society at risk, there was not as much of a danger. It seems to me that if we send out a signal that white collar crime is not as serious in the community, we tend to promote the idea that someone will tamper with this white collar crime because the sentencing is not as severe, and even if that person is sentenced there is really no form of incarceration or no sentencing that is going to have a sustained penalty.
White collar crime is really serious in this country today. If we send out a signal that we are not going to really consider this crime as just as dangerous to society

November 4, 1991

as some of our other crime, we are not going to do anything about minimizing its presence.

Yes. I am not suggesting for a moment that white collar crime is not important and does not hurt people in a material way. I am suggesting that there are other ways of punishing many of those who have offended as white collar criminals other than putting them in our prison system. That is what I have said.
Repayment is one way of doing it, if it takes a lifetime. My God, what a sentence to repay the money stolen by fraud or by cooking the books.
I also want to make it very clear that I am not including organized white collar crime in that category.

Mr. Speaker, having been a prosecutor and a defence counsel, I am hard put to find out where exactly the member is coming from. It seems to me that what he is really saying is he likes the status quo just the way it is in the criminal justice system, in which case I would ask him if he has ever spoken to a victim or to the family of someone who has been raped or murdered. What planet is he living on when he gives a speech like that?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Very briefly, the hon. member for Brant.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad I only have a brief time. A question like that really does not warrant any kind of intelligent answer.
I am just as concerned about the hapless victims of violent crime as any other reasonable human being is. The question, as phrased by that member, unfortunately is all too common from that seat and is not worthy of a responsible answer.

Mr. Speaker, I understand I am allowed 20 minutes. I only have 15 minutes before Question Period resumes. I hope you will allow me time later to finish. I will do my best to tell the reasons why I am supporting this bill fully, the corrections and conditional release bill.
The role of government is a lot of things, such as providing a framework for economic prosperity, providing infrastructure to support all citizens in their efforts to develop skills in order to play an active role in society, and providing social programs to provide the basic needs
Government Orders
for Canadians. It must also provide a system of fair laws that are enforced by the courts and police and provide for the safety and well-being of our people. It is this issue of safety of security of Canadians that we are addressing today.
For the past seven years, since I was elected in 1984,1 have served on the Standing Committee of Justice and the Solicitor General. For the past two and one-half years I have chaired that committee.
It is a great honour for me to chair that committee, because it is the first time in the history of Parliament that committee has ever been chaired by someone other than a lawyer. I am not a lawyer. I will admit that lack of legal knowledge is somewhat of a hindrance in that capacity.
However, I do have great support from the legal system such as the very fine clerk who is a lawyer and some people from the Library of Parliament who are lawyers and who assist me and make it very easy for me to operate this committee. I am very hopeful that this bill will be referred to our committee because I feel we have an area of expertise developed through which we can give a fair hearing to this bill.
I listened with great interest to the Solicitor General, the hon. member for York South-Weston and the hon. member for Brant giving their various positions. Some of them surprised me.
I joined the justice committee the same day as the hon. member for York South-Weston. He talked at great length about the Taking Responsibility report which was a unanimous report of that committee. At no time did that report say we should get rid of parole or mandatory supervision. As a matter of fact, it stated we should keep parole and mandatory supervision.
Now he says that he believes we should get rid of them. I do not believe it will serve any purpose. During crime prevention week this government is moving to bring in bills that I have been advocating since the day I came here.
People will agree that the most interesting work that MPs carry out is the work of standing committees. I also have found it rewarding, but sometimes frustrating. Frustration comes when, after months of research and hearings, a document is produced and tabled in Parliament and it receives limited acceptance from the

November 4, 1991
Government Orders
government. We have had this happen. It happened with numerous situations we have studied.
I have openly criticized the government for failing to adopt the recommendations produced by committees, not only the justice committee but other committees. These reports collect dust in a maze of bureaucratic bookshelves. This is not the case with this bill.
Let me explain exactly what happened. We were asked by an order of reference from the House of Commons to study Bill C-67. We studied it. We came up with 16 recommendations. We tabled a report in the House of Commons. The government came back and accepted 13 of those recommendations and many of them have been integrated into Bill C-36, the corrections and conditional release bill.
Canadians have always felt threatened by a parole system that jeopardized their safety. Other people have spoken of the Gingras case. It is absolutely ludicrous that we should have a justice system where a murderer, who is known to be dangerous, should be allowed to go to the West Edmonton Mall to celebrate his birthday, overpower a guard, and murder two more people. One man was shot in the back of the head, execution style, and a young girl was strangled with her own shoelaces. This is a terrible, terrible situation.
There has been reference to the Legere case. There were mistakes made there. It is no wonder that the public does not have confidence in the judicial system, in the penitentiary system that they should have.
There is talk about a 99.93 per cent success rate. Any failures are too many and this bill goes a long way.
Let me tell you other things the government is doing. The importance of public safety is reflected in other areas. The firearms legislation restricts possession of dangerous weapons and provides better screening of firearms acquisition applications. Surely that will help. It is supported by so many people, the police chiefs association, among others. We are bringing in amendments to the Extradition Act to allow a more streamlined extradition process to prevent criminals from using our courts to avoid facing criminal charges in other countries. Is there something the matter with this? Why should Canada keep Charles Ng and Joseph Kindler in this country?
Who is bringing it forward? This government is bringing it forward. Canadians have witnessed a disturbing increase in violent acts carried out by young people. Bill C-12 proposes amendments to the Young Offenders Act allowing the courts better flexibility in sentencing youths who commit murder. Bill C-30 is before my committee right now. We will be meeting Wednesday morning on clause by clause study. We hope to report to the House very soon. There was great to-do made about being late. We were late not because we could not have reported on time, but because committee members would not come out and go through clause by clause. That will be done Wednesday morning. I just want to point that out to the hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam. I hope he will be there Wednesday morning at 8.30.
Our commitment to public safety is clear and is reflected not only in Bill C-36 but in these other bills as well. I do not need to go through the highlights of this: the victims of crime to be formally recognized, judges may delay parole eligibility of violent offenders and serious drug offenders to half the sentence, and so on.
Other members have gone through a review of the literature on this thing. Let just read you a few of these things. I am quoting from The Ottawa Sun of October 10, 1991:
But remember we are living in a world where justice reform continues to move, sometimes rightly, it must be said, in the favour of the accused and the convicted. It is an achievement for the Tories to come up with a bill that would increase sentences for violent offenders and give victims a bigger say in how long they stay in jail.
This is the important part. He is referring to the fact that it took this Tory government to make even these few changes in favour of victims. "Mr. Nunziata", and I am quoting so I have every right to use his name, "can call the proposed legislation weak-tinkering by a weak minister, but it was the Liberal years in power which led to the tipping of scales in favour of criminals. While the NDP has given cautious approval to Lewis' bill, judging by the party's general policies, one suspects they would have followed the Liberal route if they had ever managed to gain office".
I will grant you there has been a terrible increase in crime. Last year there were 270,000 violent crimes in Canada, well above the 219,000 average for the 1985 to 1989 period.
November 4, 1991

There were 60,101 youth cases heard in Canada, 9,013 for violent offences, an increase of 14.7 per cent. This is why we have to bring in amendments to all of these bills.
I just want to go through what some people say about this bill. Gary Rosenfeld, executive director of Victims of Violence International, said in an interview from Ottawa that the proposal is a helluva step forward. He is confident that most government and opposition MPs will support it.
In The Times Colonist on Saturday, October 12, 1991 it is described as sensible and overdue.
The bill which Mr. Lewis said could be law by next spring is being described as the first comprehensive review of the Penitentiary Act since 1868. It also proposes the greatest changes in the parole system since the Parole Act was passed in 1958.
We heard this morning that the hon. member had a chance to read The Toronto Star.. I wonder what other papers he does read. But The Toronto Star cannot find anything wrong with the bill. It did not say anything bad about it. Even the The Toronto Star cannot say a bad thing about it. "Tougher parole planned". Not a bad thing about it.
Is this a speech or an apology?

It is certainly not an apology. It is no apology at all. It is an apology for what your government has done to take away victims' rights. I want to tell you that the only way to wipe the smirk off the criminal face of this nation is to come down hard and long.
What we were pleased to see in Lewis' bill, however, is the recognition of victims' rights finally. Their voice should be the loudest voice heard.
I could go on and on with these reports from what various people say about this bill. As legislation goes, this is not a highly partisan issue, at least it should not be, and the Lord knows there are enough lawyers in Parliament to offer ideas. The ideas will come when this bill goes to committee.
I would recommend that without further speakers we refer this to the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General. Let us make the few small amendments we have to make. Mr. Speaker, I would like to recommend that this bill be referred to-

The
member seemed to suggest that we on this side of the House were not supporting the general thrust of this legislation. I would like to clarify that. For our side of the House, we are supporting reform here. However, we also believe there are areas in this package that can be improved.
I have a specific question for the member. Do you not find it a little bit contradictory that during this week of safety in the streets, crime prevention, we come before the House with all kinds of legislation, yet at the same time you cut the budget by $2 million in terms of a National Crime Prevention Week? Is there not a little bit of a contradictory action there?

Mr. Speaker, we do not like to see any reduction in the moneys that will be spent for National Crime Prevention Week. We certainly abhor having to make these deductions, but we were left with an horrendous debt which must be reduced. Mr. Speaker, today I rise to honour the victims of last week's Hercules air crash on Ellesmere Island.
I also want to pay tribute to the rescue team. This tragic event of life and death and survival is filled with

November 4, 1991
S. ft 31
heroism. We know from the survivors that there was courage and caring and selflessness of the highest order.
We honour all these brave men and women, those who lost their lives, those who survived and those who gave their lives so that others might survive.

Mr. Speaker, Saturday night, at the 16th Annual Convention of the Gens de Tair, it was my privilege to award the Prix BILCOM 1991 to Didier Feminier, a federal public servant.

Our sincere congratulations to Mr. Feminier and to the two winners of the Prix Roger Demers, Pierre J. Jeanniot and Pierre Rivest-

Mr. Speaker, for the last year and a half, the farming community has been waiting anxiously for the Atlantic Livestock Feed Initiative phase II agreement, better known as ALFI II.
This program was put in place in order to help Atlantic farmers reach self-sufficiency in grain production. It is extremely important for the future of agriculture in Atlantic Canada.
At the present time, Atlantic farmers pay a lot more for their feed grains than other Canadian farmers because of the very high transportation costs. ALFI II will help our agricultural community to become less dependent on transportation costs.
A couple of weeks ago, the Minister of Agriculture decided to maintain the ALFI II program for Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island.
I call on him now to make a positive decision for New Brunswick because Atlantic Canadian farmers are awaiting his decision.

Mr. Speaker, I have a statement.
Before I give it, I would like to acknowledge what the member from the Arctic said. I hope the government or perhaps even the Speaker as well would speak on behalf of the House for that heroic rescue.
My statement is on another matter.
The government announced a law and order agenda for Crime Prevention Week.
Canadians want strong measures to keep our country safe, but this Conservative agenda is as phoney as a $3 bill. I call it the blue box agenda. All these measures are basically recycled bills.
The Young Offenders Act, Bill C-12, was tabled in 1989 and cleared a committee a year later. It could have been called any time in the last year.
The same with the mental disorders act. It was drafted in 1986, and only a court decision forced the tabling. Also, with extradition, it is being delayed. Gun control is being watered down to satisfy the gun lobby.
If you want to prevent crime, let us be honest: You tackle illiteracy, you tackle child abuse, you tackle poverty and unemployment, you control guns and you face up to the problem of domestic violence.
November 4, 1991

That is the way to tackle crime, and the government should get serious about it.

Mr. Speaker, for decades the residents of Stewiacke, Nova Scotia have been fighting for improved safety at the very dangerous rail crossing in their town which has been the scene of many accidents, injuries and deaths.
I am pleased to report that the system works. Even though Stewiacke is not a major city, not even a major town, it got the attention of the Minister of Transport and his officials who have just announced that safety will be improved at this crossing. The plan includes a realignment of the intersecting roads, the installation of barrier gates and an educational program for students in the area. A cost-shared program has been proposed with the federal government assuming 80 per cent of the total cost. On behalf of the people of Stewiacke, I want to thank the Minister of Transport for his personal attention to this matter and the quick and positive action which will now result in a much safer crossing.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, seven years ago today the Tory government released its blueprint for action: "A New Direction for Canada: An Agenda for Renewal". That document urged that Canadians brace themselves for unbounded prosperity. Their new government was to ensure that Canadians could compete on world markets. Indeed, that same view was widely expressed by the Prime Minister during the election campaign in 1988.
Canadians know that prosperity is not unbounded. We are in a recession. The government's plans for increased competitiveness have led to the deindustrialization of Canada's manufacturing heartland. After seven years of gross mismanagement, the government has finally realized what Canadians have known all along. Its policies have been disastrously wrong.
Now it will spend $25 million of our money asking Canadians to tell it what it should do. This is not a government capable of leading anybody anywhere. Before it wastes any more money, it should resign and allow the people to elect a group of men and women of ability, many of whom now sit on the opposition benches in this House.

Mr. Speaker, a high school student put it very well when he said: "Be cool, finish school". Canada Career Week is being held November 3 to 9. As part of the national stay in school initiative, Canada Career Week theme is "Start to finish". The emphasis is on students finishing high school and pursuing post-secondary education in a career he or she has chosen.
By the year 2000 it is estimated that two-thirds of all new jobs will require at least grade 12 schooling, and fully 40 per cent will require 16 years of schooling. These statistics only serve to illustrate the need for the government's stay in school program.
This government will continue to promote this initiative by strengthening partnerships between business, educators and young people. Youth are our future. We must ensure that they are well prepared to meet the challenges of the 21st century.
speakername: Mr. Walter Van  De Walle@St. Albert

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, November is Migraine Awareness Month. Migraine is a far more serious and costly condition than many imagine. Almost 3.2 million Canadians over the age of 15 suffer from some form of migraine. Doctors are still unsure about what causes the attacks. Seventy-seven per cent of migraine sufferers have had to restrict their normal activities because of an attack.
There is currently no universally effective medication available for migraine, although many migraine sufferers can learn how to recognize what triggers the problem and regain control over their lives. The occurrence of migraine in Canada has a significant economic impact. Almost 4 million work days a year are shortened or lost due to migraine, resulting in an annual work place productivity loss of almost $500 million.
The purpose of Migraine Awareness Month is to focus public attention on this devastating problem. I urge all

November 4, 1991
members of Parliament and all Canadians to support the Migraine Foundation in its efforts to promote awareness of migraine and the appreciation of its impact on its sufferers, their families and on society as a whole.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Speaker, I rise to express my concern about a federal government employee passing on to the media that the federal government might be considering a fee to be paid by cross-border shoppers to help pay for the emergency farm aid package. Today I would like to voice my strong opposition to such a measure. A surtax at the border will be interpreted by my constituents as a simple action by the federal government to inhibit cross-border shopping.
What we need are policies which address the roots of our uncompetitiveness, not measures which can be interpreted as attempts to close off or set up artificial road-blocks. A levy of this type also appears to overlook its potential impact on our customs officers. It would increase their workload significantly and seems to me runs counter to our efforts of maximum efficiency.
I strongly believe our government must not be entertaining any notion of a levy or fee on cross-border shoppers. I hope that members of the House of Commons will join with me in voicing their concern on this important matter.

Mr. Speaker, just last week a spokesperson for a Vancouver based company confirmed that they are proceeding with plans to construct a dam near Valemount, British Columbia, on the North Thompson River, which is a tributary of the Fraser River, in an effort to divert water flow into the Columbia River watershed and then using a series of canals and pipelines to transfer this water into southern California.
This is part of a plan to divert a number of western Canadians rivers into the southwestern United States and northern Mexico known as the North American Water and Power Alliance Proposal.
Canadians have always been worried that the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement may eventually end up giving Americans access to our fresh water and now, with the Canada-U.S.-Mexico negotiations under way, the worry is even greater.
Water is not another commodity to simply sell to the United States. It provides the very lifeblood for a delicate ecosystem.
Therefore, I call upon the Prime Minister and the Government of Canada to state categorically that our waters are not for sale, that our waters will not be dammed and diverted into the United States.

Mr. Speaker, during the last few months, the citizens of Delta have become more and more concerned about the increasing violent crime and vandalism in our community. I am sure the people of Delta will be encouraged by the federal government's initiatives recently introduced before the House, as well as those forthcoming changes which will be proposed in the near future.
Changes to the Young Offenders Act were long overdue. I am also pleased with the amendments to the extradition laws and to the Corrections and Conditional Release Act.
While controversial in many areas, the firearms legislation is a step forward in controlling violent crime and the use of dangerous weapons.
The government is to be commended for taking these steps to protect its citizens against those who would abuse the freedoms we have and destroy the way of life and freedom which we cherish. Law-breakers in Canada must be made responsible for their own actions and
November 4, 1991

Canadians must again be able to feel safe on their streets and in their homes.

Mr. Speaker, the Cyrus Eaton group has offered to buy the American Piper Aircraft Corporation and move it to Canada where it could eventually employ some 3,000 people.
Experience shows that for every job created in the aircraft industry, two more jobs are created in supply and service industries. Because of Canada's relatively high wage rates, we need high tech jobs such as those in the aircraft industry if we are going to compete internationally. Jobs like this are particularly important right now because the Toronto area alone has lost 175,000 jobs during the past year and now has double digit unemployment.
The government must do everything possible to encourage Piper to come to Canada. Let us not blow this one.

Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands-
Canso): Mr. Speaker, the jobless situation in my constituency of Cape Breton Highlands-Canso and indeed all across Cape Breton Island is reaching crisis proportions.
Instead of acting to alleviate this situation, this government is putting additional road-blocks. A good example is the changes to regulations and procedures for qualifying and receiving UI benefits in the wake of Bill C-21. Not only have the provisions for receiving UI been tightened, but the red tape required to explain and administer these new rules has created additional barriers.
As a result, the numbers of unemployed calling on the services of our local CEIC and Revenue Canada offices to deal with outstanding claims has multiplied in recent months. The resources to deal with this demand simply cannot cope. Constituents are waiting six to eight months for decisions to be rendered by understaffed government departments.
Several months without a decision on an unemployment insurance claim quite simply can mean several months without money for rent, food and clothing.
When will the ministers of these departments act to cut back on these lengthy delays?

Mr. Speaker, I rise to pay tribute and honour to the brave men and women of the Canadian Armed Forces who, over the last few days, were part of a tragic accident and an heroic rescue in the high Arctic.
For more than 30 hours, a group of survivors of the crash of a Hercules aircraft struggled to cling to life. Outside the fuselage were the bodies of four others who made the ultimate sacrifice for their country.
Overhead and ready to leap into the blindness of an Arctic storm were search and rescue technicians who did not blink in the face of an incredibly dangerous and selfless assignment.
'There are many heroes in this story, but none greater than the captain of the aircraft, John Couch. In the words of his co-pilot, Lt. Joseph Bales: "If anybody was a hero it was John Couch who threw so much into surviving and keeping us going and keeping people organized. If you are going to paint anybody a hero you should paint John Couch. He worked the whole time like an extremely dedicated professional. He just did not give up one single bit and when he had finished helping others, John Couch closed his eyes and died".

Mr. Speaker, according to The Toronto Star, the Minister of Justice has announced that this week the Commons will have a blitz of law and order legislation. Last week we had a conference here on Canada's children and they reported that one child in six in Canada is poor, that half of the Canadians who rely on food banks are children. There are still more poor children than there were 10 years ago, that many poor children in families are struggling on 50 to 60 per cent of poverty line income and that in 1988 almost two-thirds of the children in families headed by single mothers were living in poverty, that more than half of all aboriginal children in Canada are poor.
How about equal time for the children of Canada? If we can afford a week of legislative time to blitz for law and order, how about two weeks for our children?

Mr. Speaker, I simply cannot believe this government's continued refusal to recognize merchant seamen as veterans. With what went on in the other place, it is evident to me that there is no commitment on the part of this government to recognize these people and extend their rightful benefits to them.
I am particularly upset that even though support for such recognition has come from all quarters, the government continues to turn a deaf ear to this serious problem. The invaluable contribution made by the merchant seamen during the Second World War must be recognized by the Government of Canada. More than 45 years have passed since the end of that war and time has definitely arrived for this government to take the just and long overdue step of recognizing the efforts of the merchant mariners as veterans.
I strongly urge the government to take prompt action in recognizing the heroic contributions made by merchant seamen to the war effort by extending to them the full range of veterans' benefits.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the Elouse to Canada Career Week which will take place from November 3 to 9. It is a national event that promotes the importance for young Canadians to focus on future careers while they are still in school.
This year's theme, Start to Finish reinforces how important education is to career planning. Communities all across Canada are pitching in to stage a range of imaginative events such as career fairs, exhibits, poster contests and conferences. Students, teachers, parents, the government and the business community are all taking an active role in helping young Canadians to look ahead to their career opportunities and a smooth transition from school to work.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. Every day Canadians are saying that the main problem facing the country now is the state of the economy. However, the government doesn't seem to listen. This morning, for instance, workers in the construction industry in Quebec heard some bad news: one-third of these workers are unemployed, and the situation is expected to get worse in the months to come.
At this very moment, unemployment is also widespread in the pulp and paper and forestry industries. Yesterday, lay-offs were announced in Dolbeau, in the riding of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and there will be more. And at this point, all the government has to offer in the way of programs is publicity stunts.
When will the government, the Deputy Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance start concentrating on the real problems that concern Canadians, and when will they take steps to ensure that our goods are competitive, instead of keeping the dollar at 90 cents as they are doing now?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I indicated to the House on Friday, the economic strategy of the government is to bring down inflation and inflationary pressures so that interest rates can come down. That is the key to economic recovery.
The hon. member shakes his head negatively but I hope he would not disagree with the fact that interest rates in Canada have come down by over six percentage points. The spread has narrowed and continues to do so. As long as we can continue on that track, I am sure the hon. member will agree that that is the recipe for economic recovery.
I am sure that he will also be interested in knowing that today, for the fifth consecutive month, the leading composite indicator, which covers everything from housing to stock markets, has again shown an
November 4, 1991

increase of 1 per cent. That is the broadest rate of growth in six years, and the hon. member should be applauding that rather than criticizing it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister does not realize that the survey of 153 companies showed that corporate profits are down 33 per cent across the board, down 88 per cent in mining, down 47 per cent in his own province in oil and gas, down 29 per cent in manufacturing products. Everything is down.
We still have a dollar that is around 90 cents. Interest rates are down in Canada, yes, but they are down in the United States and the spread is still the same.
When will he change his policies and make Canadian products competitive so that Canadians can go back to work? They have been out of work for more than 18 months as a result of the policies of this government.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure what the policy of the federal Liberal Party is with respect to the exchange rate. The last I heard it is the same policy that the hon. Leader of the Opposition had when he was finance minister. He said back in 1978, and I quote: "We believe that market forces should continue to determine the appropriate exchange value for our currency. What we are doing as we have done consistently for the past eight years is to smooth out erratic fluctuations in the value of the dollar as they occur in the marketplace". That is precisely the policy of the federal government.
The issue is not to manipulate the exchange rate. He knows that. If he is calling for a fixed exchange rate or if he is calling on us to adopt the American currency as our currency, why does he not stand up and say so. Canada is sovereign in its own power to determine and maintain the value of the currency and that is one of the most fundamental aspects of any economic and monetary policy.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):

Mr. Speaker, the main economic problem we face is that the people of Canada want to work today. Everybody knows, and every commentator says that the Canadian dollar is too high. The only recipe this government has at this
Oral Questions
moment is to maintain the high dollar and to put forward their advertising campaigns. The only people doing well these days in Canada are the people in advertising.
There was a program for advertising the Constitution last month. There was one on productivity last week. There is one this week on law and order. When will the government give jobs to Canadians, and not only the people who are friends of its party who work in the advertising business?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the hon. Leader of the Opposition might advise us what his policy is with respect to the exchange rate.
If he does have a view on the value of the dollar, what is it? How would he get it there and how would he keep it there? Perhaps he might want to take us into his confidence and advise the House. Come clean with Canadians. Do not just stand there. You cannot have it both ways.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
Gaines Pet Foods Corporation of Cobourg, Ontario, employs 110 people, exports two-thirds of its product, yet faces a crisis today because of the high dollar.
Despite aggressive business strategies, the company tells me it loses $150,000 in potential profit for every penny increase in the value of the Canadian dollar, causing Gaines a $1 million profit loss this year alone.
Gaines has to make an important decision; stay here or shift its production to the United States. What is the minister's advice to Gaines Pet Foods Corporation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is more to being competitive than just simply looking at the exchange rate. There are many components that go into making a business competitive and productive and show a profit.
The hon. member does express a point of view and it is one that concerns us all. There is in fact a depression in commodity prices throughout the international marketplace.

November 4, 1991
Oral Questions
I remind the hon. member that our merchandise trade balance for this year is $8.1 billion. The merchandise trade balance rose $8.1 billion at an annual rate to $13.5 billion in August. That would indicate to me, Mr. Speaker, that Canadian concerns are in fact meeting competition. They are cutting their costs. I am sure that with the reduction in interest rates, the lessening of inflation and inflationary pressures, that competitive opportunity will be all the more fruitful for them.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is to the same minister. I would be happy to share with the minister the fact that statistics show that this company has been very aggressive and has taken on some very innovative policies to improve its ability to compete.
Gaines Pet Foods Corporation is in jeopardy; 110 jobs in a small Ontario community are in jeopardy. Across Ontario, over one-third of our businesses are looking to moving out. Staying here means shutting down.
Will the government explain why it refuses to take direct action to lower the Canadian dollar or provide other emergency relief today to Gaines and other Canadian businesses in distress because of the high dollar, in order to give them a fighting chance to survive here in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have taken definitive action, first of all, in bringing down inflation and inflationary pressures and the corresponding reduction in interest rates that have come down by over six percentage points. That trend is continuing. We have addressed the problem of prosperity and competitiveness. Of course that is an issue that all Canadians must face in the form of a partnership.
The hon. member talks about all the firms that are leaving the country. I said in the House the other day that Chrysler Corporation was putting a third shift on its Windsor plant for the manufacturing of mini-vans.
Imperial Tobacco announced a $16 million retooling and expansion plant in Elgin-Norfolk County about two weeks ago.
Dupont Canada triples profit. It is adding that the free trade agreement with the United States enabled the company to boost its profits.
Piper Aircraft, Mr. Speaker, chooses Canada. Dupont opens a world-scale plant.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Acting Prime Minister. Contrary to the Deputy Prime Minister's statements, this country has lost 410,000 jobs because of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement.
Bankruptcies are near an all-time high. Le Soleil has just done a poll which shows that most Canadians are opposed to the Canada-U.S. deal and are opposed to the Mexican deal.
You better believe it.

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister this question. Is he prepared to table in this House all the documents, all the research and all the back-up papers that this government has prepared in dealing with the Canada-U.S.-Mexico deal. Where is the evidence that Canada will benefit out of this proposed deal? Are you prepared to document it?

speakeroldname: Hon. William C. Winegard (Minister for Science):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in terms of the free trade agreement we already know that over the last two years our exports to the United States have increased substantially. Interestingly enough, some of our exports to other parts of the world have not increased at all. Surely that would tell you that the free trade agreement as such with the United States is working.

Mr. Speaker, I did not wish to embarrass the government, but now I am compelled to.
Mr. Speaker, in my hand is a document the government spent-
The hon. member knows the rule against using props. Perhaps the hon. member will put his question.

Mr. Speaker, I will not use a $1 million document presented by the government as a prop, even though I may think it is a crock. But, Mr. Speaker, in the document that the taxpayers of this country paid $1 million for, Mr. Porter says unequivocally that thousands of jobs have left Canada because of the free trade agreement, and I refer to page 69. This is not my
November 4, 1991

argument but Mr. Porter's argument in this document which I will not use.
I put the question to the Deputy Prime Minister. In face of this government's own evidence after spending $1 million on the Porter report, what research is available to this House and to the people of Canada that shows that entering into an agreement with Mexico will be any better than the one we got with the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. William C. Winegard (Minister for Science):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is quite interesting that members opposite did not want a free trade agreement with the United States presumably because the United States would outgun us with its high-tech and its power. Now they do not want a free trade agreement with Mexico for exactly the opposite reasons.
It is kind of hard to know what they really do want.
Mr. Speaker, what the Canadian people want is the 410,000 jobs back right now.
Hear, hear.

What the Canadian people want back are the industries and the spinoffs we once had from those branch plants. What we want is our place in the economy.
I ask the Deputy Prime Minister whether or not this government is prepared to table all the documents and research it has done, if any, which show that the Mexican deal will be a good one.

speakeroldname: Hon. William C. Winegard (Minister for Science):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is kind of interesting to go back and look at what we wanted out of the free trade agreement with the United States.
We wanted for example a dispute settlement mechanism, which we got. We wanted economic benefits, which we have and I have just given the numbers. We wanted market access, which we have got.
Just last Friday afternoon I had a firm in my office in Guelph saying: "The reason we are here talking to you is because of the FTA". I said: "Come on and talk some more".
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
Over the last two years this government has increased UI premiums by 44 per cent to $1.95 per $100 in 1989 to $2.80 per $100 in 1991.
Given the desperate state of third-quarter profits of Canadian businesses outlined by the Leader of the Opposition, given that Canadian workers in this country are already taxed to the teeth, will the Minister of Finance tell this House, and through this House tell Canadians, that the government will say no to an increase in UI premiums at this time?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would only indicate that while premiums have indeed gone up so have benefits. Benefits have improved by about 55 per cent. As I indicated in the House the other day-
Nonsense.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Hon. members say: "Nonsense". They may just want to check their facts and figures on this because that has in fact occurred.
With respect to UI premiums, as I indicated in the House the other day there is a process where the recommendations are brought forth by the commissioners for ratification. I have not received such a recommendation at this time.

Mr. Speaker, the only thing the government accomplished in Bill C-21 was to withdraw the government from funding of the unemployment insurance account and to force the unemployed to pay for their own retraining program. That is all the government accomplished, and the minister should admit it up front.
Given that 10,000 Canadian small businesses must change their computer software to accommodate any change in the UI premium, a change that is supposed to be legally in place by January 1, will the minister tell the House today that there will be no increase in the UI premium? Will he make that news available to the Canadian business community as soon as possible, a

November 4, 1991
Oral Questions
community that is bleeding under excessive taxes and poor fiscal and monetary policy by this minister?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have indicated to the hon. member earlier that I have not received a recommendation from the commissioners. There is a process that is to be followed and we will follow it in the usual manner.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport.
As he will know, the shipbuilding industry in this country has been brought to its knees by the government of which he is a member. The national ship building policy that was promised by his Prime Minister in 1984 during the election is nowhere in sight.
Will the minister undertake now to wipe out all the tariff exemptions on boats entering Canada? Will he now require that all fishing boats fishing in Canada be built in Canada?
Mr. Speaker, I can tell the hon. member that one thing we are thinking about is making sure the ships of one of his fellow members eventually bear the Canadian flag.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary for the same minister.
The minister can create a lot of confusion and wave his arms, but the fact remains that thousands of construction workers are unemployed, all because of this governe-ment's broken promises.
Will the minister implement measures today to guarantee that all goods now being shipped between domestic ports are carried by ships built in Canada, manned by Canadian crews and sailing under the Canadian flag?
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to offer my sincere congratulations to the hon. member opposite who, like many of his colleagues, has been practising in front of a mirror. I am sure I will never achieve his degree of skill in making gestures, but I
repeat that perhaps he could use his influence on his colleague to ensure that owners of Canadian ships start by flying the Canadian flag.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
According to confidential briefing note JLO-1006, a U.S. submarine made an illegal submerged passage through Canada's internal waters at Dixon Entrance in June 1990. On Friday the minister denied knowledge of the matter despite the fact that a formal written protest was made by External Affairs.
Is the minister suggesting to the House that last Wednesday she approved blanket consent for U.S. nuclear subs in Dixon Entrance without knowledge of the earlier illegal activity?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member would reflect on what was actually said on Friday, what I said was: "Not to my knowledge but I will look into it".
Indeed there were transits through the Dixon Entrance in 1989 and in 1990. There was a formal protest lodged by the department through diplomatic notes and indeed that led to the discussions which enabled us to provide guarantees for Canadians as a result of the new policy and the co-operation on the disputed waters.
I think that the hon. member should at least be relatively more open about his questions.

I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker.
It is the minister who signed the Order in Council on Wednesday providing blanket prior consent for the U.S. subs to go through Dixon Entrance, and on Friday she was trying to tell Canadians she had no knowledge of previous illegal activities by the U.S. sub fleet.
During the furious debate over Arctic sovereignty on the illegal voyage of the Polar Sea in March 1987, the right hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs gave categoric assurances as found in Hansard that "there will be no secret agreement sprung upon anybody" and to

V:

********
November 4, 1991

"consult extensively with all those Canadians who are interested".
Why the double standard on Dixon Entrance: no consultation and a secret agreement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was hardly a secret agreement since we announced it.
What we did was get guarantees from the U.S. concerning the transits through Dixon Entrance because the United States co-operated with us. We had registered protests. The Department of National Defence found out through normal discussions with the U.S. defence authorities the potential for SEAFAC. We were able then to get some guarantees from the U.S. as a result of that, and then we announced it. It was hardly a secret agreement.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. In his annual report the minister announced that he intended to facilitate access to this country for immigrants with a trade, at the expense of the family reunification program. How will the minister explain to a mother who has been waiting two years for her son to come to Canada, that she will now have to wait a little longer because the government has changed its priorities?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know the hon. member and I am sure he would not want to mislead his fellow citizens. The proposed changes certainly do not imply there will be a longer wait for family reunification in Canada, but that is what the hon. member is trying to make people believe. I hope he will correct this impression.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the minister increases the independent class it automatically decreases the family class because the
Oral Questions
number is now fixed. Maybe he should read his annual plan closely.
Family reunification has taken a back seat to the Tory economic agenda as a top priority of Canada's immigration law. How can the minister justify increasing entry into Canada of other groups when it now takes three years or more for a husband and wife to be reunited in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it takes some gall. I mean this is the political party, following the tabling of the immigration level for the year, which said that the family class was in jeopardy.
In the family class this year 100,000 people will come into Canada for family reunification. Perhaps I could just add this: in 1984 the Liberal Party that formed the government at that time was welcoming 88,000 people to Canada. This year we will be welcoming 250,000 and I do not think that he should be complaining.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister concerning the environment.
Evidence from the government's own environmental experts shows conclusively that 47 pulp and paper mills using chlorine bleach are pouring toxic substances into Canadian waters.
Since the Minister of the Environment agrees that the entire effluent from these mills is poisoning fish and causing birth defects, why has the government refused to regulate these substances and protect our water from these poisons?

Mr. Speaker, I say to the hon. member that we will be bringing forth very shortly the new pulp and paper regulatory issues. The substantial increase in the AOX, which is the 350 chemicals within that effluent, will be decreased substantially to 2 kilograms per tonne from 5 kilograms per tonne which was in 1988.
I think the member will see on the regulatory system that is coming in very shortly that we will have good success on that.

November 4, 1991
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, the minister of state is referring to regulations that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has been sitting on for over four months.
We are talking about something different. We are talking about toxic substances and the entire toxicity of effluent from mills. Knowing this, knowing that the entire effluent is toxic, will the minister of state admit that the Minister of the Environment has made a mistake by saying he will not regulate this effluent? Will she assure the House that regulations will be brought in?

Mr. Speaker, yes, I will assure the member that regulations will be brought in concerning dioxins and furans. That is going to have a substantial effect on the whole soup of chemicals of the AOX. We expect about a 60 per cent decrease in all of those.
At the present time there is a tremendous amount of research going on in terms of the kind of process to have the paper the whitish colour that we want, the substitute for the Kraft process. There is a process going on in British Columbia which is really quite excellent. We are pleased about that. The peroxide and the ozone being used in that process is certainly a result of some good technology.
I am veiy pleased that science and technology is doing a $60 million report on some of the new technology that can be used in order to reduce this effluence.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Associate Minister of National Defence.
I am sure all members of the House and all Canadians will join in offering our deepest condolences to the families of those who were killed in last week tragic accident near Alert and paying tribute to those who were involved in the heroic effort to rescue the survivors.
Major Lloyd Clifton, the chaplain at Canadian Forces Base Edmonton, said yesterday speaking of Captain John Couch's self-sacrifice: "It is the kind of stuff the Victoria Cross is awarded for".
Will the government be considering giving this country's highest honour to those who were involved in that heroic effort, in particular to the late Captain John Couch?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again I thank my hon. colleague for his thoughts.
As I said in the House on Friday, I know that all hon. members join in condolences to the families of the five who lost their lives in this crash and to the survivors. I had a chance to visit with most of them this morning and talk to them. They are coming along very well. What they went through in this ordeal is an incredible story. Of course we also express appreciation to the search and rescue people who did an outstanding job.
I know all of these issues will be reviewed. Where honours can appropriately be given, I can assure my hon. colleague that appropriate consideration will be given to that.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for that as do all members of the House.
I would just like to ask a follow-up question. On Friday the minister indicated that there was a report being prepared on the causes of the accident. As the minister knows, four other Hercules were involved in earlier crashes. There have been some questions arise about the cause of this, about the adequacy of the equipment available, about the potential involvement of the Innu people in the rescue operation, and various other questions.
Will the minister table a report on all of these issues with the standing committee on national defence so that the committee can decide whether a further public inquiry can take place on the events surrounding this accident?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a board of inquiry which has been established to investigate what the causes of the accident were and what the contributing factors were. The black box has been found and interviews of course will take place with all the survivors and others involved.
November 4, 1991

I think it is too early to say just how long that process will take. Obviously it has to be a thorough process. As in the past the information about the causes of the crash will be made available to the public and to the standing committee in the course of making that information public.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister who is acting on behalf of the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology.
The American Piper Aircraft Corporation has offered to create up to 3,000 jobs in Canada and has indicated at the same time that it would prefer to do so in the Toronto region.
I would like to ask the minister if it is true that the government is trying to discourage Piper from establishing in the Toronto region? If it is not, what is the government doing to help Toronto get those jobs?

speakeroldname: Hon. William C. Winegard (Minister for Science):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful for the opportunity to respond to that question because neither Investment Canada nor the Department of Industry, Science and Technology attempts in any way to indicate where it would be most appropriate for businesses to locate in Canada.
In this particular instance the company wanted to know something about regional development programs, so WED and ACOA were there to provide that kind of information. We certainly do not want in any way to be directing jobs to Toronto, to Montreal or to any other place.
It happened that in this instance there was no provincial representation at all on the request for people to go down to Florida to talk about this issue.
We understand that there has been no deal made at the present time and that there are still four countries in the running for this particular plant.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Forestry I will put my question to the Deputy Prime Minister.
Oral Questions
The Deputy Prime Minister knows that the Canadian forestry industry today is facing the worst crisis with the lowest commodity prices in a decade, with a countervail duty on softwood lumber and with an overvalued dollar.
In the face of this crisis the government has reduced the support program for its federal-provincial forestry agreement with the province of Ontario by 66 per cent from the previous five-year agreement.
I wonder why the government is cutting support to an industry like this that is drowning in a sea of red ink.

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to tell my hon. friend, who should be aware of this since his riding is in northern Ontario, that we announced this morning, the provincial government of Ontario and the Government of Canada, a major new agreement for northern Ontario: $95 million over the next four years. It includes a large forestry component which the Minister of Forestry also signed this morning.
This will give a tremendous boost to forestry in northern Ontario and is just one tangible example of the kind of action the hon. member is looking for. He should have been aware of that announcement this morning.

Mr. Speaker, the problem is that the people in northern Ontario are too aware of an agreement that cuts support by 66 per cent.
I would like to ask the minister about the forestry agreement. The previous agreement planted hundreds of thousands of hectares of seedlings to reforest areas in northern Ontario. Why, in an agreement that was signed today in Sault Ste. Marie, is some 12 per cent of the agreement being spent on public relations and advertising rather than on long-term benefits to an industry in very serious trouble?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the problem with the party opposite in just about every industrial component in the Canadian economy is that they overlook the importance of research. They overlook the importance of new technological adaptation. They overlook the importance of developing consciousness among the people of Canada about how to improve the industry and to make it more competitive.

November 4, 1991
Oral Questions
That is what this agreement does.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture and it refers to the commitment to expand the Nappan Experimental Farm in Nappan, Nova Scotia.
Although the commitment was reaffirmed in March of this year the original commitment was made in 1986.1 do not want to rush the minister, but I wonder if he could indicate when this important project might proceed.

I can
inform my colleague, Mr. Speaker, that Nappan is in a group of 10 research stations which we studied. I can inform him also that further to that study as to necessary capital expenditure, some $100,000 has been spent to upgrade Nappan research station. We have identified other research locations which must be included in the study. Public Works has been contracted to carry the studies out, and we hope to have our major capital construction plan available for the hon. member before the end of fiscal year 1991.

Mr. Speaker, one of the most important concerns of Canadians right across the country is the increase in crime, whether it be in our urban centres or in rural communities. Canadians are concerned about the proliferation of guns and drugs in their communities.
This week is Crime Prevention Week. At a time when the government says it is concerned about the increase in crime in our country, it has totally slashed, cut the budget for Crime Prevention Week.
I would like to put this question to the Deputy Prime Minister. Can he explain why at a time when Canadians are crying out for reform, at a time when Canadians are crying out for some leadership from the federal government, that this government has totally eliminated the budget for Crime Prevention Week?

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if my hon. friend had reviewed the 1991-92
Main Estimates he would have seen that in fact the announcement was made at that time that our participation in National Crime Prevention Week was going to be eliminated. Contrary to media reports the figure is not $2 million. The funding was in fact $340,000.

Mr. Speaker, the fact is that the government is not contributing one single solitary cent to Crime Prevention Week, and that is the travesty.
Canadians are concerned, and in particular in metropolitan Toronto. As of yesterday there were 74 murders this year already in metro Toronto. The previous record was 60 for all of 1987, and there are still two months to go in this year. Canadians are concerned about crime prevention.
I would like to put this question to the Deputy Prime Minister. When is this government going to show some leadership as far as criminal law reform is concerned? If it is truly concerned about criminal law reform, why has it cut completely the budget for Crime Prevention Week? Why has the government totally washed its hands of criminal law reform?

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend not only missed the Main Estimates. He missed the question immediately in advance of his question from the hon. member for Algoma wherein the whole point of the Liberal Party was: Why are you spending money on public information?
In fact many of the original aims of National Crime Prevention Week are completed. We have outside groups involved in it. For that reason, since they are working with police forces across Canada, we decided to use our money elsewhere.

Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George -Bulkley
Valley): Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister in the absence of the Minister for International Trade.
It concerns the softwood lumber tariff memorandum of understanding. News reports have quoted Canadian officials as saying that the government was going to present Canada's case on the softwood lumber tariff and
November 4, 1991

its dispute with the United States to GATT. Given the high dollar and the loss of many jobs in this important sector, can the minister confirm whether this is actually happening and/or what steps the government is taking to fight this regressive action by the Americans?

speakeroldname: Hon. William C. Winegard (Minister for Science):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have said in this House before that we are taking every step we possibly can under the free trade agreement and under GATT to ensure that this memorandum of understanding causes us no further difficulty.
We believe that there are no subsidies in the Canadian softwood lumber industry and we believe we can prove it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister.
Canadians are concerned that this government will sell out Canada's forest industry as it did in late 1986 when this was negotiated before.
My question is: Can the minister tell this House and Canadians, all of those people who are involved in these negotiations, to have the broadest possible consultations? Would he speak to his colleague, the Minister for International Trade, and have the minister appear before the Commons forestry committee to give a detailed briefing to members so we might be aware of the complete approach the government is taking on this?

speakeroldname: Hon. William C. Winegard (Minister for Science):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what the government is doing in this instance is precisely what industiy wanted us to do. It wanted us to take this approach.
I remind the hon. member that in terms of the countervail in 1986, the methods we are now using going through the free trade agreement were not available then. We wish they had been.

Mr. Speaker, despite very low interest rates and lower real estate prices now, a lot of would-be, first-time home buyers have a tough time raising the capital for a down payment. My question is for the Minister of Finance. Can he tell the House what the status is of proposals to allow the use of RRSP funds for the purchase of homes by first-time buyers?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's ongoing interest in this very important subject.
As he knows this is a proposal that has been brought forward by the Canadian Real Estate Association. I have had officials in the Department of Finance examining this very closely. I am myself somewhat intrigued by the idea and the principle.
My understanding is that the finance committee is going to be studying this issue as well. I certainly look forward to its views and recommendations on that. As soon as this review is completed I will be in a position to advise the hon. member and other hon. members in the House.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
Last Friday, the minister again proceeded with a unilateral announcement, over the objections of the government of Quebec and that province's employment minister. The minister announced another occupational training program, although he knows perfectly well that in Quebec there is unanimous support for patriating all this money to make the program more effective.
My question is this: Why this unilateral gesture, which is an insult to all groups in Quebec, since they are all agreed the minister should get out of this area?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, regarding the government initiative referred to by the hon. member, when he says that the provinces were not consulted, he should recall, if that is not too much trouble, that when we proposed amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act by tabling Bill C-21, all the provinces, employers and unions in this country were consulted. In fact, they indicated that they approved of these amendments, and on that basis, decisions are being made on how to make the allocated funds productive. The Bloc Quebecois is

November 4, 1991
Points of Order
asking us to let Canadian workers suffer for the sake of the constitutional process, at a time when these measures are needed to train the labour force in Quebec and the rest of Canada.
I wish to draw to the attention of members the presence in the gallery of His Excellence Sir Clement Maynard, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs of Commonwealth of the Bahamas.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, you will be aware that on last Wednesday evening during the course of the taking of a vote on a private member's matter concerning senior citizens a number of members raised the very point that they were unable to vote because the vote occurred slightly earlier than they had anticipated.
Without casting aspersions on anyone, I would simply like the House to know that we intend to pursue the matter and to raise it at the House management committee where the rules are being reviewed to make sure that members are not prevented from voting on matters and that if we have a repeat of that incident we will all know precisely when the vote will occur.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I may remind the hon. member that I was in the chair during that incident. My ruling was that the Speaker had no choice but to proceed with the vote when, in accordance with the Standing Orders, the two Whips indicated to the Speaker that members on both sides were ready to vote.
If hon. members wish to change the Standing Orders, I think the hon. member made a very good suggestion, and perhaps the committee could consider this matter. That being said, I do not think there can be any further
discussion in the House about the incident and the ruling I made last week.

subtopic: USE OF FRENCH IN THE HOUSE
USE OF FRENCH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I imagine that during Question Period, you also noticed the valiant efforts of the hon. member from Burin-St. George's in French. In fact, I strenuously object to the fact that the Minister of Transport and other government ministers laughed at the hon. member's performance when he made a very special effort to speak French. Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: USE OF FRENCH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: I am not sure what part of the Standing Orders the hon. member is referring to.

subtopic: USE OF FRENCH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: I am referring to the fact that the Speaker asked us to show some decorum and respect for other members in this House during exchanges in the course of debate, and the leader of the government did as well. Today we witnessed a valiant effort while the other side of the House indulged in rude behaviour. I think that if we want both languages to be used in the House we should respect those who make the effort.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
