Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to follow up on the question I asked in the House on June 4, 1991 concerning the Canadian government action, jointly with the United States, to protect the Great Lakes.
Let me begin by reminding the House of the significance of the Great Lakes. These contain 20 per cent of the world's fresh water supply, the largest reservoir of drinking water in the entire world. They are the major source of drinking water for more than 26 million people on both sides of the Canada-U.S. border. If we include the St. Lawrence River as part of the Great Lakes basin, it is 40 million people.
Now the bad news. It is estimated that between 400 and 500 spills of hazardous substances occur into the Great Lakes every year. Toxic substances such as PCBs and DDTs have been linked to reproductive failure, population declines, developmental abnormalities and generational defects in fish and wildlife.
This summer's report of the International Joint Commission made it clear that the condition of the Great Lakes is a threat to the health of our children. It is producing infertility in adults. It is producing reproductive damage, poor verbal and memory skills in some 4-year olds and weakened immune systems.
Many of the scariest chemicals in the Great Lakes can be traced to one source, pulp and paper mills on the Great Lakes which use chlorine for bleaching. Along the St. Lawrence tributary rivers, and the Great Lakes themselves, 73 pulp and paper mills, out of the 150 in Canada, are discharging into those waterways. In Ontario alone nine mills are discharging 200,000 pounds a day of chlorinated organic substances into the waterways.
In the face of such alarming and well-known statistics, the government has still failed to announce a joint plan with the United States that was promised for last December, put off until March and in April postponed indefinitely. The goal is zero discharge.
Adjournment Debate
Even Lake Superior, a relatively pristine lake in the Great Lakes system, is still not protected to the extent it should be within the commitments that Canada has made under the international water quality agreement it has with the United States.
It is now September and the government has failed to protect the Great Lakes and other waterways in Canada, even from dioxins and furans, the first two substances it should be regulating under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act which was passed in 1988.
This week we heard the minister say that even though it has been proven that the entire effluent of chlorine used in pulp and paper mills is a toxic substance and he recognizes that, he will not regulate the effluent from pulp and paper mills using chlorine.
We have seen the loss of wetlands in the basin and now we have Great Lakes United going to the United Nations. This is a binational organization that is concerned about the protection and clean-up of the Great Lakes. They are saying that deadline after deadline under the international agreement between Canada and the United States has been missed. It is going to the United Nations to ask it to investigate. Surely it is time for the government to protect this international resource.

The people of Croatia in June voted 94 per cent in favour of independence. The Yugoslav army has refused
to recognize the validity of that vote and is using its armed might to move into Croatia and undermine the possibilities for the people of Croatia to have independence.
Unfortunately the world community has been powerless to prevent massacre, slaughter, innocent loss of life by innocent people, the destruction of some of the treasures of the world in Dubrovnik and there is no sign that I can see, and I hope the parliamentary secretary will be able to bring some news of hope, that there is some potential solution. We see almost weekly new announcements of cease-fires and nothing has happened.
There are three specifics that I asked the Prime Minister about on October 8 that I hope the parliamentary secretary can address in his reply to these comments. First, the question of humanitarian aid. The government did provide for some humanitarian aid through the International Red Cross, but reports out of Croatia say that humanitarian aid is not arriving in Croatia. I suggested at the time, and our party has put forward the proposition, supported by the Croatian Canadian leadership in this country that the aid should be routed through Slovania.
I would like to ask the parliamentary secretary to say whether any effort has been made by the Canadian government to route humanitarian aid through Slovania. I would like to ask whether any effort has been made to increase the aid from the amount announced. I think it was $250,000. Clearly the situation is they are heading into winter and the situation is going to be desperate for hundreds of thousands of people, many of whom have relatives here.
The second point I would like to ask the parliamentary secretary about is economic sanctions and what has happened about economic sanctions. We had today in respect of Haiti an announcement of economic sanctions imposed there. The government was quick to support economic sanctions against Iraq. What is happening about economic sanctions?
The third question I would like to ask is what diplomatic initiatives is Canada taking within these days? We know about the diplomatic initiatives before and we fully support that. We know the strong statements the Prime Minister has made on this issue. We know the initiatives the government took a while back to have the matter

raised at the United Nations. What I would like to know is what is happening now when the situation is desperate.
I would like to see what initiatives the government is taking in recent days and proposes to take in the days ahead to try to head off further catastrophe and to give some hope to the people of Croatia.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Plourde (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of International TVade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may point out first of all that since the beginning of the Yugoslav crisis, Canada has spoken out firmly against the excessive use of force as reflected in the actions of the federal Yugoslav army in Slovenia and subsequently in Croatia.
Since June 27 this year, our government has criticized the use of the Yugoslav armed forces. In recent weeks, according to all observers, the army has reacted with a force out of all proportion to the acts of aggression committed against the army. Elowever, we must not assume that all parties have been guilty of breaking the many cease-fire agreements to which they were committed.
We have indicated on several occasions that strict and unconditional observance of cease-fire agreements is an essential condition for seeking a negotiated settlement. Canada still believes a comprehensive solution to the crisis is possible. I am referring to the twin track approach adopted by Serbia and Croatia on October 4. We believe that concentrating on a single aspect of the problem, such as withdrawal of federal forces, is not likely to be helpful in reaching a comprehensive settlement. An agreement between the Yugoslav republics should involve a set of guarantees including protection of human rights and minority rights and respect for the principles of international law.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has already announced publicly that Canada was prepared to join the international community in imposing economic measures on those parties that obstructed the peace process. To be effective, such measures must be taken in close co-operation with all trading partners of the parties involved. Since Canada's economic ties with Yugoslavia are relatively modest, we can only act in consultation with our European partners, preferably under the aegis of the UN Security Council.
Adjournment Debate
If the House gives its unanimous consent, I would like 30 seconds to deal with a question that was raised by the hon. member with respect to Canada's contribution.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is there unanimous consent?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Economic sanctions should only be applied if political negotiations fail. They must be imposed carefully to ensure that they have the desired impact, which in a federate country in that part of the world is not assured.
As you know, Canada contributed $250,000 to the International Committee of the Red Cross for Yugoslavia. We believe that the Red Cross is respected by all for its impartiality in providing services to those in greatest need. The Red Cross with its six local offices in Croatia and Serbia is the best way to send our humanitarian aid. We will keep in touch with the ICRC and the UN High Commissioner for Refugees to assess their needs.

Mr. Speaker, on October 7, 1991, I asked a question that I think I have asked three or four times. I have not received the answer in Question Period. Perhaps in adjournment proceedings the parliamentary secretary will give more specifics, so I am looking forward to the response.
My question is with regard to the Canadian steel industry that everyone agrees is certainly at peril. It is the cornerstone of any country's manufacturing and everyone agrees that the steel industry in Canada is at peril.
I have spoken, no doubt, regionally and parochially about Algoma Steel at length, but also recognizing that Sysco Steel in Nova Scotia is about to close or possibly it shall close, and most of the other major steel producers in Canada are losing money. They are losing millions of dollars and in some cases hundreds of millions of dollars.
For one year now at Algoma the problem has been very real. It is a crisis that continues. I do not know if the community can withstand the crisis on an ongoing basis. We have lived from deadline to deadline, extension to extension. The last time we made a request to the federal government was for a $10 million loan guarantee. At that time, they waited and waited and spoke and said we are talking to players. They talked it out and there was no $10 million loan guarantee.

November 4, 1991
Adjournment Debate
This time we are again on a deadline. We are looking at December 16, an extension, to take a look at the restructuring of Algoma. We all recognize and we all know that there will be less people working at Algoma. I have asked the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology on numerous occasions as well as his senior staff what the federal government is prepared to do. It has suggested that it is still talking with all of the players and it is waiting yet again until the final proposal comes forward.
It is difficult for a community to stand on the edge for one year, and December 16 is precariously near the Christmas season. We would like some specifics from the government. I know it cannot say it will address 2,000 people for retraining and it will address 575 older working people under the older workers adjustments program, but it can do more than just say it will continue to talk with the players and it will help where it can help when the restructuring is in place.
I ask the parliamentary secretary to respond on behalf of the minister. Can he give us some specifics? Forget the generalities now and say that, yes, we are prepared to get involved in tax credits so that employees may buy out an ailing company. Just follow the Ontario government lead.
Will the government recognize the older workers adjustment package and introduce some flexibility?
I met with the Minister of Labour and he suggested that some flexibility is possible.
Will the government offer any assistance in some pension enhancement so that we can get older workers to step aside for younger workers so that the community is not really decimated with all of the young families forced to relocate?
I ask the parliamentary secretary if he can give us any indication, any solace, that there are some definite specifics in mind that the federal government is considering.
